program_title: Neurodiversity, Trauma-Informed Practice & Complex Behavioral Needs

metadata.target_audience: Parents and caregivers of neurodivergent youth, traumatized youth, or children with complex behavioral needs (Ages 4–18)
metadata.core_objective: Differentiate skill deficits from willful defiance, adapt boundaries for executive dysfunction, and apply trauma-informed co-regulation.
metadata.key_deliverable: Accommodated Accountability Plan & Collaborative Problem-Solving Worksheet

topics.title: Skill Deficit vs. Willful Defiance
topics.summary: Re-framing non-compliance as executive dysfunction or neurological overload.
key_principles: Kids do well if they can (Dr. Ross Greene framework).
Executive function deficits require structural scaffolding rather than punitive measures.

topics.title: Trauma-Informed Boundaries & Meltdown Management
topics.summary: Differentiating tantrums from involuntary neurological meltdowns and maintaining connection before correction.

activities.title: The Defiance vs. Skill Deficit Audit
activities.instructions: Re-evaluate recurring conflict flashpoints through a neuro-affirming lens and build environmental accommodations.

tasks.title: Collaborative & Proactive Solutions (CPS) Execution
tasks.action: Complete a 3-step CPS plan (Empathy, Adult Concern, Invitation) for a chronic household struggle.

quiz.question: How does a sensory/neurological meltdown differ fundamentally from a tantrum?
options: A) Meltdowns only occur in teenagers; tantrums occur in toddlers.
B) A tantrum is goal-directed and driven by the conscious brain, whereas a meltdown is an involuntary fight-or-flight overload response.
C) Meltdowns require harsher consequences to prevent repetition.
D) There is no difference between the two terms.

quiz.question: What is the most effective initial approach when holding a trauma-impacted child accountable after a boundary violation?
options: A) Removing all privileges immediately for 30 days.
B) Establishing felt emotional safety ('Connection Before Correction') before addressing the behavior.
C) Speaking louder so they understand the severity of their mistake.
D) Sending them to their room until they write an essay.
